summary: This benchmark investigates transplanting the final feed-forward layer of a smaller 0.5B model (Qwen2.5-Coder-0.5B) into a larger 1.5B model (Qwen2.5-1.5B) to evaluate whether a frozen subnetwork can recover loss after block ablation. The experimental methodology is remarkably rigorous and honest, featuring extensive controls (shuffled donor, direct affine bridge, non-coding 0.5B donor), though it lacks code verification and shows negative/marginal practical utility.
strengths: Exemplary experimental design featuring sound negative and ablation controls (shuffled donor, direct affine projection, general base donor).
Highly candid and scientific presentation of results without overhyping; clearly notes that routing failed to specialize and that most recovery came from linear projection maps.
Precise reporting of metric units, confidence intervals, sample sizes, and model architectural dimensions (1,536 channels for 1.5B, 896 for 0.5B).
weaknesses: Absence of a verified supporting repository in the submission metadata limits direct independent verification (text_only badge).
Evaluations are limited strictly to token loss/perplexity on small windowed slices of CPython rather than standard downstream code execution or reasoning benchmarks (e.g., HumanEval, MBPP).
The core practical result is largely negative: the intact native model easily outperforms the graft, and the domain-specific donor provides negligible advantage over a general-purpose donor.
suggestions: Provide the supporting repository directly for artifact verification to obtain the verified_open badge.
Evaluate functional downstream generation metrics (e.g., pass@k on HumanEval or Python code completion) in addition to next-token cross-entropy loss.
Explore transplanting earlier or middle MLP layers, as final layers often have idiosyncratic alignment with unembedding layers.

claims.text: The host has 1,536 channels and the donor 896.

Model stitching and sparse upcycling provide related precedents for connecting pretrained components and deriving experts from dense checkpoints. [Model stitching](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.07682) · [Sparse upcycling](https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.05055).
When the host’s original block was removed, an aligned donor recovered 40.3% of the increase in next-token loss on Python code and 26.3% on documentation.
claims.source: Internal experimental calculation based on reported table values: (1.978 - 1.807) / (1.978 - 1.554) = 0.171 / 0.424 = ~40.3%

novelty_vs_existing.title: Revisiting Model Stitching to Compare Neural Representations
novelty_vs_existing.contribution: Applies cross-model stitching ideas specifically to transplanting single FFN blocks between unequal-width LLM architectures (1.5B vs 0.5B) rather than stitching entire sub-networks at equivalent depths.

novelty_vs_existing.title: Sparse Upcycling: Training Mixture-of-Experts from Dense Checkpoints
novelty_vs_existing.contribution: Evaluates cross-model heterogeneous donor block transplantation into an existing dense model rather than cloning homogeneous MLP layers to build a sparse MoE.
